whatItDoes: Applies one or more discount percentages in sequence to a starting price and shows the final price, the total amount saved, and the effective discount percentage. Discounts stack multiplicatively: a 20% off + 10% off stack is 28% off, not 30%.
whyItExists: Most shoppers intuitively add discount percentages, but stores always apply them in sequence. A 20% + 10% coupon is 1 − 0.8 × 0.7 = 0.44, so 44% off, not 30%. This calculator shows the real final price for any stack of discounts, the actual dollar amount saved, and the effective percentage so you can compare to 'X% off' offers.
whoShouldUse: Shoppers comparing stacked coupon offers, retail marketers designing promotion campaigns, e-commerce analysts evaluating discount effectiveness, and small business owners sanity-checking sale pricing.

commonMistakes: Applying in the wrong order: stores usually apply the larger discount first
Forgetting the order: the same set of discounts applied in a different order gives the same result mathematically, but the line items may differ
Confusing 'X% off' with '$X off' — 20% off $100 = $20, but $20 off $100 = 20%
Trusting advertised 'up to X% off' — the average is much less than the maximum
Rounding after each step instead of at the end — small errors compound over many discounts
faq: How does stacking work? — Each discount multiplies the running subtotal. A 20% discount on $100 leaves $80; a 10% discount on that leaves $80 × 0.9 = $72. The final is 1 − (0.8 × 0.9) = 1 − 0.72 = 0.28 of the original, so 28% off.

Why is 20% + 10% = 28% and not 30%? — Because each discount is taken on the running total, not the original. $100 × 0.8 × 0.9 = $72, which is 28% off the original. Adding the percentages would only work if the discounts applied to non-overlapping portions of the price.

Does the order of discounts matter? — Mathematically no: multiplication is commutative. In practice, stores always apply the larger discount first, so the line items differ. The final price is the same either way.

What about 'BOGO free' (buy one get one free)? — That depends on the relative price of the two items. The simplest case (BOGO where the second item is the same price) is 50% off if you buy 2. For mixed carts, treat each line as its own discount calculation.
Is this calculator accurate? — Yes, uses standard arithmetic with full floating-point precision. The displayed values are rounded for readability; the final price is exact to 2 decimal places.
